title: Free build week two: the plan meets the world
summary: Build the core of your own project first, hit the first real wall and let the bug diary carry the fixes, then check what the week's changes cost against the cap.
materials: your free build parts, bought against the cap
your build plan and priced materials list from week 9
pencil and paper for the budget check
phone or camera for the progress photo

steps.title: Build, test, fix
steps.body:
The design loop: ask, imagine, plan, build, test, fix. Last week you did ask, imagine and plan: you picked the person, picked the problem, drew the plan and priced the list. The pay yourself first money is already set aside and the parts are on your desk. This week the loop reaches its favourite part: build.

One rule keeps this week from wobbling: build the core first. The core is the one part that must work for your build to be your build at all. If your project holds something, the core is that it holds without falling. If it lights up or makes sound, the core is one light or one sound doing its job on command. If it is a program, the core is the shortest version that does the main thing once. Everything else, the paint, the decorations, the extra features, is frosting, and frosting waits.

Say your core out loud in one sentence before you touch a single part. If the sentence has an and in it, it is probably two things, so pick the one the whole build leans on.

One more promise to make now, while everything still smells like a fresh plan: something this week will not work on the first try. That is not a maybe. When it happens you will not have a disaster, you will have an entry for the bug diary, and the diary is where fixes come from.

Five minutes of typing, hands on the home row, eyes on the screen. Today's words are the bug diary's words: expected, happened, tried, changed, fixed, next. Type each word five times. Then type this whole sentence twice without looking down: I expected one thing, I got another, and I changed one thing at a time.

steps.title: Build the core
steps.body:
Set your plan from week 9 where you can see it. Point at the part of the drawing that is the core, the one part the whole build leans on, and build only that.

Work in small rounds: add one piece, then test what you have, then add the next. Testing after every piece sounds slow, but it is the fastest way there is, because when something breaks you already know which piece broke it: the one you just added.

If a part does not fit, or a step in your plan turns out to be wrong in the real world, do not quietly swap in a different part and move on. Write the change on a change list, one line each: what the plan said, what you did instead. That list is not a list of mistakes. Plans meeting the world always bend, and Friday's budget check needs to know exactly where yours bent.

Stop the round the moment the core works once, and take the photo right then, first working moment, mess and all. If the core is still not working when the hour ends, photograph it exactly as it stands instead. Either photo is one your science fair board will want, because both of them are true.
checklist: I said the core in one sentence before building, and it had no and in it
I added one piece at a time and tested between pieces
Every change from the plan is on the change list, one line each
I have a photo or screenshot of the core, either the first moment it worked or exactly how far it got today

steps.title: The wall, and the diary that eats it
steps.body:
Somewhere in the building, the wall shows up: the part that refuses to work, the piece that will not fit, the code that does the wrong thing on purpose. When you hit it, do not push harder. Open the bug diary and feed the wall to it.

An entry has four lines. What I expected. What happened instead. What I tried. What happened then. Then the golden rule from every robot and circuit you have ever fixed: change one thing at a time. If you change two things and it starts working, you do not know which change fixed it, and worse, one of the two might be quietly breaking something else.

Give the wall at least two honest, logged tries before you call for a grown-up. When you do ask for help, bring the diary and read it out: here is what I expected, here is what I tried. You will sound like an engineer, because that is exactly what engineers sound like.

If the wall still stands at the end of the session, that is allowed. Write the exact question you are stuck on as the diary's last line. A wall with a precise question in front of it is already half fallen, and week 11 gets another swing.
checklist: The wall is written down: what I expected and what happened instead
I made at least two fix attempts, changing one thing at a time, each one logged
I asked for help only after my second logged try, and I brought the diary
The diary ends with what fixed it, or with the exact question I am stuck on

steps.title: Why things break where pieces meet
steps.body:
Take a strip of scrap paper and pull it apart with your hands. It takes a real tug, and it tears somewhere random. Now take a matching strip, cut one tiny notch in its edge, and pull again. It gives up easily, and it always tears at the notch.

Here is why. When you pull on the paper, the pulling force spreads out across the whole strip like traffic across many lanes. A notch, a corner, a hole or a joint closes lanes, so all the force crowds into the little bit of material that is left. Engineers say the stress concentrates there. That is why things snap at corners, crack at screw holes and fail at glue joints: not because those spots are unlucky, but because that is where the force piles up.

So when your build breaks, look first at the places where two pieces meet. And the strange thing is, this is true of programs too. Two halves of a program can each be perfect, and the bug lives at the seam where one half hands its answer to the other and the two halves disagree about what that answer means. Joints and seams, wood or code: check where the pieces meet first.

steps.title: The budget check
steps.body:
Time to let the numbers catch up with the week. Put three things side by side: the priced list from week 9, your change list from the building, and your receipts or leftover money.

Go down the change list and give every change its price. Some changes cost money: a part that broke and needs a second one, a swap to a dearer piece. Some changes save money: a part you found at home, a decoration you dropped. Write the number next to each change, plus or minus.

Now work out the new total and set it next to the cap. Remember the order from week 9: the pay yourself first money came off the top before the shopping started, and it stays off the table now. It is not a rainy day fund for parts.

If the new total still fits under the cap, say so out loud and enjoy it. If it does not, the budget decides, not the wish: something gets cut or swapped for a cheaper way, and you choose what. Finish either way by writing one line: the thing I would cut first if the cap gets tight. Deciding that now, while you are calm, is a hundred times easier than deciding it later in a hurry.
checklist: Every change on the change list has its cost or saving written next to it
The new total is worked out and sits next to the cap
The pay yourself first money is still untouched
I wrote the one thing I would cut first if the cap gets tight

steps.title: Planned price versus real price
steps.body:
The item bought stays fixed for each row, since this compares one part's planned price against what it actually cost. Only the source of the number, plan or receipt, changes between the two columns.

One row per item actually bought this week, at least three items. For each row, write the item, its planned price from week 9, and its real price from the receipt.
steps.question: Which item cost more than planned, and by how many dollars?

steps.title: Show it
steps.prompt: A photo or screenshot of your core, either the first moment it worked or exactly how far it got today, a photo of this week's bug diary page, and a photo of the budget check sheet with the new total next to the cap. If your build is a program, paste the core code or a share link too.
